lessons.title: Solving the PDE: How the Closed-Form Formula Falls Out

children.text: "You have the equation," the interviewer says. "Solve it." This is the lesson every other lesson in this course has been building toward: turning the Black-Scholes PDE and its boundary condition into an actual number you could quote on an options desk. The route taken here does not touch the heat-equation transformation Black and Scholes originally used. It stays inside stochastic calculus, using a result that converts the entire differential equation into something this course already knows how to compute: an expectation.

body.text: The Black-Scholes PDE, together with its boundary condition, is equivalent to a discounted expected payoff, computed under a version of GBM where the drift is replaced by the risk-free rate r. Working out that one expectation, for a call option's lognormal payoff, is a completing-the-square calculation away from the world-famous closed-form formula.

children.text: From PDE to Expectation: The Feynman-Kac Shortcut

A result called the Feynman-Kac theorem connects a PDE like the one from the previous lesson to an expectation of the boundary condition, computed under a modified process where μ is replaced by r. This lesson takes that connection as given; the next lesson explains rigorously why it is valid.

body.latex: C(S,t) = e^{-r\tau}\, E\big[\max(S_T - K,\ 0)\big], \qquad S_T = S\, e^{(r - \sigma^2/2)\tau + \sigma\sqrt{\tau}\, Z}, \quad Z \sim N(0,1)
body.caption: The Feynman-Kac connection: μ replaced by r, then discount the expected payoff

body.text: Compare this to Lesson 1's formula for S(T). It is identical, with one single substitution: μ has become r. That substitution is exactly the missing-μ observation from the previous lesson, now put to direct use, and the next lesson unpacks precisely why it is legitimate.

children.text: Splitting the Expectation Into Two Pieces
max(S_T - K, 0) equals S_T - K whenever S_T > K, and 0 otherwise. Splitting the expectation along that same condition turns one messy expectation into two more tractable ones.

body.latex: E\big[\max(S_T-K, 0)\big] = E\big[S_T \cdot \mathbb{1}_{S_T > K}\big] \; - \; K \cdot P(S_T > K)
body.caption: Splitting the payoff's expectation into two separate pieces

children.text: The Easier Piece: P(S_T > K) = N(d2)

This is exactly Lesson 1's standardization technique, reused directly. S_T > K exactly when ln S_T > ln K, and ln S_T ~ N(ln S + (r - σ²/2)τ, σ²τ) under this risk-neutral drift. Standardizing gives a clean normal-distribution probability.

body.caption: The easier of the two pieces, a direct standardization

children.text: The Harder Piece: E[S_T · 1(S_T > K)] = S e^(rτ) N(d1)

This piece needs one more step: multiplying a lognormal variable by an indicator before taking its expectation shifts the effective distribution being integrated against, a technique often called exponential tilting. The clean way to see it is a completing-the-square argument on the integral's exponent. The full algebra is shown below for anyone who wants to see every step; the result is what the rest of this lesson uses.

body.title: Show the full derivation (completing the square)

children.text: Let X = ln S_T ~ N(m, v), with m = ln S + (r - σ²/2)τ and v = σ²τ. The piece needed is E[e^X · 1(X > ln K)], written as an integral against X's normal density.

content.latex: E\big[e^X \mathbb{1}_{X>\ln K}\big] = \int_{\ln K}^{\infty} e^x \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi v}} e^{-\frac{(x-m)^2}{2v}}\, dx
content.caption: Step 1: the integral to be evaluated

children.text: Combine the two exponents, x and -(x-m)²/(2v), and complete the square in x. The algebra rearranges the exponent into a new, shifted normal density plus a leftover constant term that does not depend on x.

content.caption: Step 2: completing the square shifts the mean from m to m + v

content.latex: E\big[e^X \mathbb{1}_{X>\ln K}\big] = e^{m + v/2} \int_{\ln K}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi v}} e^{-\frac{(x-(m+v))^2}{2v}}\, dx = e^{m+v/2}\, P(Y > \ln K)
content.caption: Step 3: the integral is now a probability for a shifted normal Y ~ N(m+v, v)

children.text: Standardizing P(Y > ln K) gives N((m + v - ln K)/√v), which is exactly N(d2 + √v) = N(d1), since d1 = d2 + σ√τ = d2 + √v by definition. And the leftover constant, e^(m+v/2), simplifies directly: m + v/2 = ln S + (r-σ²/2)τ + σ²τ/2 = ln S + rτ, so e^(m+v/2) = S·e^(rτ).

content.caption: Step 4: the harder piece, fully evaluated

body.latex: E\big[S_T \cdot \mathbb{1}_{S_T>K}\big] = S\, e^{r\tau}\, N(d_1), \qquad d_1 = d_2 + \sigma\sqrt{\tau} = \frac{\ln(S/K) + \big(r + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\big)\tau}{\sigma\sqrt{\tau}}
body.caption: The harder piece, stated for the main derivation to continue

children.text: Substitute both pieces back into the split expectation, then discount by e^(-rτ). The e^(rτ) from the harder piece and the e^(-rτ) discount factor cancel exactly, leaving the closed-form formula in its familiar shape.

body.latex: C(S,t) = e^{-r\tau}\Big[S e^{r\tau} N(d_1) - K N(d_2)\Big] = S\, N(d_1) - K e^{-r\tau}\, N(d_2)
body.caption: The Black-Scholes formula for a European call option
The d1 and d2 formulas, in their standard form

children.text: Worked Example: Pricing the TCS Call

body.caption: Inputs for pricing a 3-month TCS call option
Pricing the call analytically, then confirming it with a risk-neutral Monte Carlo simulation
body.code:
import numpy as np
from math import log, sqrt, exp, erf

S, K, r, sigma, tau = 3900, 4000, 0.07, 0.24, 0.25

def norm_cdf(x):
    return 0.5 * (1 + erf(x / sqrt(2)))

d1 = (log(S/K) + (r + 0.5*sigma**2)*tau) / (sigma*sqrt(tau))
d2 = d1 - sigma*sqrt(tau)
call_price = S * norm_cdf(d1) - K * exp(-r*tau) * norm_cdf(d2)
print(f"d1 = {d1:.4f}, N(d1) = {norm_cdf(d1):.4f}")
print(f"d2 = {d2:.4f}, N(d2) = {norm_cdf(d2):.4f}")
print(f"Black-Scholes call price: Rs {call_price:.2f}")

# Cross-check with a risk-neutral Monte Carlo simulation, back to Chapter 1's
# very first tool: simulate, then average, then discount.
n_sims = 500_000
Z = np.random.normal(0, 1, n_sims)
S_T = S * np.exp((r - 0.5*sigma**2)*tau + sigma*sqrt(tau)*Z)
payoffs = np.maximum(S_T - K, 0)
mc_price = np.exp(-r*tau) * np.mean(payoffs)
print(f"Monte Carlo call price:    Rs {mc_price:.2f}")

# Typical output:
# d1 = -0.0052, N(d1) = 0.4979
# d2 = -0.1252, N(d2) = 0.4502
# Black-Scholes call price: Rs 172.40
# Monte Carlo call price:    Rs 172.35

body.text: This closes a full circle back to the very first tool this course used. Chapter 1 opened with random walks and simulation to build intuition. This lesson's Monte Carlo cross-check uses the exact same idea, simulate, average, discount, to confirm a closed-form formula that took three chapters of stochastic calculus to derive analytically. Both routes agree, to within simulation noise, because they are answering the exact same question.

body.title: Interpret the harder piece
body.question: What does E[S_T · 1(S_T > K)] = S·e^(rτ)·N(d1) actually represent?
options: The probability that the option finishes in the money
The expected value of S_T, counted only in the scenarios where the option finishes in the money, adjusted back to today's terms
The Black-Scholes call price itself, with no further steps needed
The variance of the stock price at expiry
body.explanation: P(S_T > K) = N(d2) is the probability of finishing in the money. E[S_T · 1(S_T>K)] is a different, related quantity: the contribution of S_T's value specifically from the in-the-money scenarios, exponentially tilted by the completing-the-square argument. Both pieces are needed, and combined, to reach the full call price.

body.title: Recompute d2 for a different strike
body.prompt: Using the same TCS inputs (S = ₹3,900, r = 7%, σ = 24%, τ = 0.25), but a lower strike of K = ₹3,800, what is d2? (Use d2 = [ln(S/K) + (r - σ²/2)τ] / (σ√τ).)
body.explanation: ln(3900/3800) = ln(1.0263) ≈ 0.0260. (r - σ²/2)τ = (0.07 - 0.0288) × 0.25 = 0.0103. Numerator ≈ 0.0260 + 0.0103 = 0.0363. Dividing by σ√τ = 0.12 gives d2 ≈ 0.30. A lower strike raises d2 compared to the ₹4,000 strike's d2 of -0.1252, since the option is now more likely to finish in the money.

cards.definition: A result connecting a PDE with a terminal boundary condition to a discounted expectation of that boundary condition, computed under a modified process with drift r instead of μ.
The two standardized quantities in the Black-Scholes formula: d2 relates to P(S_T > K), and d1 = d2 + σ√τ relates to the exponentially tilted expectation E[S_T·1(S_T>K)].
The completing-the-square technique that evaluates E[e^X·1(X>a)] for normal X by shifting the mean of the integrated density by v, the variance.
C = S·N(d1) - K·e^(-rτ)·N(d2), the closed-form price of a European call option, derived from the PDE via the Feynman-Kac expectation.

points: Feynman-Kac converts the Black-Scholes PDE and its boundary condition into a discounted expectation, computed under GBM with μ replaced by r, the exact substitution the missing-μ result from the previous lesson pointed toward.
Splitting E[max(S_T-K,0)] into E[S_T·1(S_T>K)] minus K·P(S_T>K) turns one hard expectation into two solvable pieces.

P(S_T>K) = N(d2) follows directly from standardizing the lognormal distribution, the same technique from Lesson 1; E[S_T·1(S_T>K)] = S·e^(rτ)·N(d1) needs a completing-the-square argument, shown in full in the collapsible derivation.
Assembling and discounting both pieces gives the closed-form Black-Scholes formula: C = S·N(d1) - K·e^(-rτ)·N(d2).
A risk-neutral Monte Carlo simulation, using the exact same tools Chapter 1 opened this course with, confirms the closed-form answer, closing the loop between simulation and analytical derivation.
The next and final lesson steps back to explain rigorously why replacing μ with r is valid in the first place, the risk-neutral pricing argument this lesson borrowed without fully justifying.
